arXiv:2611.27865v1 [cs.AI] 20 Nov 2026

SLICR: Strategy Logic-Guided Multi-Agent
Reinforcement Learning

Arshia Rafieioskouie     Matthew Lucas     Tzu-Han Hsu     Borzoo Bonakdarpour Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering Affiliation: Michigan State University Affiliation: East Lansing, MI, USA
Abstract

Specification-guided reinforcement learning (RL) translates formal specifications of desired behavior of agents into shaped rewards. This paper introduces SLICR, a significant paradigm shift that advances the state of the art to specification-guided RL in adversarial settings under partial observability. We employ Strategy Logic (SL), which allows explicit quantification over agents’ strategies and uses the linear temporal logic (LTL) to specify the agents’ objectives and constraints. This enables reasoning not only about how agents should act to satisfy a specification, but also about how they should respond to the strategies and behaviors of other agents. We evaluate SLICR on three popular benchmarks: Predator-Prey, Google Research Football, and our home-grown extension of SMAC-HARD, demonstrating its effectiveness, scalability, and ability to adapt to diverse adversarial strategies.

1 Introduction

Specification-guided reinforcement learning has recently gained significant attention by using desired agent behaviors expressed in formal languages to guide the learning process (Alur et al., 2026). Formal specification provides rigorous syntax and semantics for reasoning about sequences of events and states over time. Recently, approaches such as (Hsu et al., 2025; Rafieioskouei et al., 2026) have demonstrated that formal specifications not only provide precise objectives for multiple agents, but also improve learning performance. However, existing specification-guided multi-agent RL (MARL) approaches (ElSayed-Aly and Feng, 2022; Liu et al., 2024; León and Belardinelli, 2020) typically assume that other agents follow stationary strategies. More specifically, these approaches have two main limitations: (1) they learn a single strategy (i.e., policy) for a fixed task or game, without explicitly adapting to the strategies of other agents; and (2) adversarial formulations often focus on rational equilibrium behavior, such as Nash equilibria (Jothimurugan et al., 2022), without considering arbitrary or irrational opponent strategies. These limitations severely limit the ability of agents to respond to a changing collection of adversarial strategies.

In this paper, we introduce SLICR (Strategy Logic-Informed Control through Reinforcement Learning), advancing the state of the art in specification-guided model-free MARL to adversarial settings under partial observability and non-stationary adversarial behavior. We employ the highly expressive strategy logic (SL) (Mogavero et al., 2014), which enables explicit quantification over multiple agents’ strategies, along with the linear temporal logic (LTL) to specify the agents’ objectives and constraints. This enables reasoning not only about how agents should act to satisfy a specification, but also about how they should respond to the strategies of other agents without making any assumptions about them. Consider the partially observable Voyage scenario shown in Fig. 1. The agents, ship () and pirate () observe only their own locations and can move between adjacent cells, except between bb and ee or hh and ee. 2 Related Work

Specification-Guided MARL.

Specification-guided MARL has been extensively studied  (ElSayed-Aly and Feng, 2022; Liu et al., 2024; Hsu et al., 2025; León and Belardinelli, 2020; Jothimurugan et al., 2022). Hammond et al. (2021) learn a joint policy that maximizes a weighted sum of the satisfaction probabilities of multiple LTL specifications.  Bozkurt et al. (2024) instead consider a turn-based stochastic game and learn a controller policy that maximizes the probability of satisfying an LTL specification against a worst-case adversary. Unlike these settings, our framework uses SL under partial observability to express richer strategic relationships. In (Rafieioskouei et al., 2026), the authors use encoder-decoder models to reason about the dependencies represented by Skolem functions. Their encoder-decoder models reconstruct the states of universally quantified trace variables to guide cooperative MARL. In contrast, we use encoder-decoder models to reason over strategies of other agents for SL-guided adversarial MARL. We believe the work most closely related to SLICR is (Hahn et al., 2024), which studies RL in fully observable settings for strategic specifications expressed in probabilistic ATL (PATL), an extension of ATL (Alur et al., 2002). Unlike SLICR, their approach supports only a single outermost strategic quantifier without alternation.

Opponent Modeling.

In SLICR, we reason about the strategies (behavior) of other agents, connecting our approach to opponent modeling. Rabinowitz et al. (2018) uses character and mental-state embeddings to represent agents’ long-term and transient behavior, relational forward models to predict future actions or returns from global states (Tacchetti et al., 2019), and hierarchical sequential variational autoencoders to infer beliefs over other agents’ strategies (Zintgraf et al., 2021). Policy representations can also be learned from observation-action trajectories, although representing unseen agents requires access to several of their previous trajectories (Grover et al., 2018). In (Yu et al., 2024), opponents’ subgoals are inferred as embeddings of future states from historical trajectories under full observability and used to condition the learning agent’s policy. Extending opponent modeling to partially observable settings, (Papoudakis et al., 2021a) reconstructs other agents’ actions and observations from the controlled agent’s local history, while (Odrowaz-Sypniewski et al., 2026) additionally models future states and returns and aggregates the resulting embeddings. In contrast, our learning is further guided by a specification and protected by a shield that excludes experiences associated with irrational strategies.

3 Preliminaries

Let Δ(X)≜{p:X→[0,1]|∑x∈Xp(x)=1}\Delta({X})\triangleq\left\{p:X\rightarrow[0,1]\;\middle|\;\sum_{x\in X}p(x)=1\right\} denote the probability simplex over a set XX, and let μ⁡(X)\mu(X) denote the uniform distribution, We abbreviate a tuple ⟨x1,…,xn⟩\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle as ⟨xi⟩i∈{1,…,n}\langle x_{i}\rangle_{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}}.

3.1 Partially Observable Stochastic Games

We model the environment as an nn-agent partially observable stochastic game (POSG) (Hansen et al., 2004). A POSG is defined as a tuple G≜⟨S,S0,A​g,A,𝐏,O,⟨Ωαi⟩i∈{1,…,n},𝖠𝖯,L⟩G\triangleq\langle S,S_{0},{Ag},A,\mathbf{P},\mathit{O},\langle\Omega_{{\alpha}^{i}}\rangle_{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}},\mathsf{AP},\mathit{L}\rangle, where SS is the set of environment states, and S0S_{0} is the initial-state distribution. A​g≜{α1,…,αn}{Ag}\triangleq\{{\alpha}^{1},\ldots,{\alpha}^{n}\} is a finite set of nn agents. We assume each agent αi{\alpha}^{i} has the same action space AA and we define 𝒜≜{𝐚=⟨a1,…,an⟩∣ai∈A}\mathcal{A}\triangleq\{\mathbf{a}=\langle\mathit{a}_{1},\ldots,\mathit{a}_{n}\rangle\mid a_{i}\in A\} as the joint action space. The transition function 𝐏:S×𝒜→Δ⁡(S)\mathbf{P}:S\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\Delta({S}), where 𝐏⁡(s′∣s,𝐚)\mathbf{P}(\mathit{s}^{\prime}\mid\mathit{s},\mathbf{a}) denotes the probability of transitioning from s∈S\mathit{s}\in S to s′∈S\mathit{s}^{\prime}\in S under the joint action 𝐚∈𝒜\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{A}. In a POSG, agents do not have direct access to the full environment state. Instead, they receive a partial observation determined probabilistically by the state and the joint action. For simplicity, we assume each agent αi{\alpha}^{i} has the same observation space O\mathit{O}. For each agent αi{\alpha}^{i}, the observation function Ωαi:S×𝒜→Δ⁡(O)\Omega_{{\alpha}^{i}}:S\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\Delta({\mathit{O}}), where Ωαi​(oi∣s,𝐚)\Omega_{{\alpha}^{i}}(o_{i}\mid\mathit{s},\mathbf{a}) denotes the probability that αi{\alpha}^{i} receives oi∈Oo_{i}\in\mathit{O} in state s∈S\mathit{s}\in S under the joint action 𝐚∈𝒜\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{A}. Lastly, 𝖠𝖯\mathsf{AP} denotes a finite set of atomic propositions, and L:S→2𝖠𝖯\mathit{L}:S\rightarrow 2^{\mathsf{AP}} is a labeling function.

Example.

The POSG for the Voyage scenario in Fig. 1 is defined as follows. The environment is a 3×33\times 3 grid world with cells labeled a,b,…,i{\it a},{\it b},\ldots,{\it i}. A​g={ship​(),pirate​()}{Ag}=\{\textsf{ship}(\raisebox{-1.72491pt}{\includegraphics[height=13.79988pt]{img/ship.png}}),\textsf{pirate}(\raisebox{-1.72491pt}{\includegraphics[height=13.79988pt]{img/pirate-ship.png}})\}. Each state is of the form (posship,pospirate)(\texttt{pos}_{\textsf{ship}},\texttt{pos}_{\textsf{pirate}}), for the position of ship and pirate, respectively, where posship,pospirate∈{a,b,…,i}\texttt{pos}_{\textsf{ship}},\texttt{pos}_{\textsf{pirate}}\in\{{\it a},{\it b},\ldots,{\it i}\}. Let (b,e)(\it b,\it e) be the initial state. Both agents can move to adjacent cells using actions A={U,D,R,L,S}A=\{U,D,R,L,S\}, except between b{\it b} and e{\it e} or h{\it h} and e{\it e}. Each agent can only observe its own current position and not the position of the other agent (i.e., O={a,b,…,i}\mathit{O}=\{{\it a},{\it b},\ldots,{\it i}\}). For example, in state s=(b,e)s=(b,e), the observations of ship and pirate are bb and ee, respectively.

A history for an agent αi∈A​g{\alpha}^{i}\in{Ag} is an observation-action sequence hαi≜oi0→ai0oi1→ai1⋯\mathit{h}_{{\alpha}^{i}}\triangleq o_{i_{0}}\xrightarrow{\mathit{a}_{i_{0}}}o_{i_{1}}\xrightarrow{\mathit{a}_{i_{1}}}\cdots, where for all j≥0j\geq 0, oij∈Oo_{i_{j}}\in\mathit{O} and aij∈Aa_{i_{j}}\in A. A sub-history hαi[ℓ:k]\mathit{h}_{{{\alpha}^{i}}_{[\ell:k]}} is a finite segment oiℓ→aiℓ⋯→aik−1oiko_{i_{\ell}}\xrightarrow{\mathit{a}_{i_{\ell}}}\cdots\xrightarrow{\mathit{a}_{i_{{k-1}}}}o_{i_{k}}, for 0≤ℓ<k<|hαi|0\leq\ell<k<{|h_{{\alpha}^{i}}|}. We denote the set of all finite histories by ℋ∗\mathcal{H}^{*}. A strategy π:ℋ∗→Δ⁡(A)\pi\colon\mathcal{H}^{*}\rightarrow\Delta({A}), where π⁡(a∣h)\pi(\mathit{a}\mid h) denotes the probability of choosing an action a∈A\mathit{a}\in A after a finite history h∈ℋ∗\mathit{h}\in\mathcal{H}^{*}. We denote the set of all strategies in GG by Π\Pi. A path in a POSG is a sequence of environment states ζ≜s0→𝐚0s1→𝐚1⋯\zeta\triangleq\mathit{s}_{0}\xrightarrow{\mathbf{a}_{0}}\mathit{s}_{1}\xrightarrow{\mathbf{a}_{1}}\cdots, where sj∈S\mathit{s}_{j}\in S and 𝐚j∈𝒜\mathbf{a}_{j}\in\mathcal{A} for all j≥0j\geq 0, and a sub-path ζ[ℓ:k]\zeta_{[\ell:k]} is a finite segment sℓ→𝐚ℓ⋯→𝐚k−1sk\mathit{s}_{\ell}\xrightarrow{\mathbf{a}_{\ell}}\cdots\xrightarrow{\mathbf{a}_{k-1}}\mathit{s}_{k}, for 0≤ℓ<k<|ζ|0\leq\ell<k<{|\zeta|}. The trace t\mathit{t} of a path ζ\zeta is a sequence of labels 𝖳𝗋(ζ)≜t(0)t(1)⋯\mathsf{Tr}(\zeta)\triangleq\mathit{t}(0)\mathit{t}(1)\cdots, such that t⁡(j)=L⁡(sj)\mathit{t}(j)=\mathit{L}(\mathit{s}_{j}) for all j≥0j\geq 0 (the trace of a sub-path, 𝖳𝗋(ζ[ℓ:k])\mathsf{Tr}(\zeta_{[\ell:k]}), is defined similarly). Notice that, we only consider valid paths and sub-paths, where 𝐏⁡(s′∣s,𝐚)>0\mathbf{P}(s^{\prime}\mid s,\mathbf{a})>0 for all transitions. We write 𝒵∗\mathcal{Z}^{*} to denote the set of all finite paths, and 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝖼𝖾𝗌⁡(𝒵∗)\mathsf{Traces}(\mathcal{Z}^{*}) to denote the set of all finite traces. Furthermore, our setting is episodic, and each episode (a finite sequence of interactions from an initial state to termination) terminates after TT steps, where T∈ℤ>0T\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}.

3.2 Strategic Logic (SL)

Syntax.

𝒯W\mathcal{T}_{W} denote ‘eventually’, ‘always’, ‘weak until’, and ‘weak then’, respectively. We say a formula φ\varphi is agent-closed if every agent α∈A​g\alpha\in{Ag} occurring in the formula is bound to some variable x∈𝑉𝑎𝑟𝑠⁡(φ)x\in\mathit{Vars(\varphi)}, and is variable-closed if every variable x∈𝑉𝑎𝑟𝑠⁡(φ)x\in\mathit{Vars(\varphi)} is quantified. A formula that is both variable-closed and agent-closed is called a sentence.

Semantics.

Let φ≜ℚ1​x1​…​ℚn​xn​(α1,x1)​…​(αn,xn).ψ\varphi\triangleq\mathds{Q}_{1}x_{1}\ldots\mathds{Q}_{n}x_{n}~(\alpha^{1},x_{1})\ldots(\alpha^{n},x_{n}).\psi be an SL sentence, where each ℚi∈{∀,∃}\mathds{Q}_{i}\in\{\forall,\exists\} and ψ\psi is the inner LTL formula. The original semantics of SL in  (Mogavero et al., 2014) is defined over deterministic concurrent games. Since we model RL environments by POSGs, we present the semantics of SL in two steps. The first step is concerned with the semantics of strategy quantifiers. The second step is related to the semantics of the inner LTL formula ψ\psi for (sampled) paths from a POSG:

— An assignment is a partial mapping 𝒳:A​g∪𝑉𝑎𝑟𝑠⁡(φ)⇀Π\mathcal{X}\colon{Ag}\,\cup\,\mathit{Vars(\varphi)}\rightharpoonup\Pi that maps each agent and strategy variable in its domain to a strategy. Given an assignment 𝒳\mathcal{X}, a strategy variable xix_{i}, an agent αi\alpha^{i}, and a strategy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, we write 𝒳[xi↦π]\mathcal{X}[x_{i}\mapsto\pi] for the assignment that agrees with 𝒳\mathcal{X} except that xix_{i} is mapped to strategy π\pi. Similarly, 𝒳[αi↦π]\mathcal{X}[\alpha^{i}\mapsto\pi] denotes the assignment that agrees with 𝒳\mathcal{X} except that αi\alpha^{i} is mapped to π\pi. We also write 𝒳[xi,αi↦π]≜𝒳[xi↦π][αi↦π]\mathcal{X}[x_{i},\alpha^{i}\mapsto\pi]\triangleq\mathcal{X}[x_{i}\mapsto\pi][\alpha^{i}\mapsto\pi]. An assignment 𝒳\mathcal{X} is complete if it assigns a strategy to every agent and every variable. We use 𝕏c\mathbb{X}_{c} to denote the set of all complete assignments and 𝒳∅\mathcal{X}_{\emptyset} for the empty assignment. The satisfaction relation is defined over a model configuration (G,Π,𝒳,i)(G,\Pi,\mathcal{X},i) and φ\varphi, where i∈ℤ≥0i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} indicates the evaluation position.

Roughly speaking, given the above semantics, our goal in this paper is to learn functions that map each existentially quantified strategy variable to a strategy in response to the choice of universally quantified strategy variables such that the probability of satisfaction of an SL specification in POSG is maximized. We will formally state this optimization problem in the next section.

4 Problem Statement

Let φ=ℚ1​x1​…​ℚn​xn​(α1,x1)​…​(αn,xn).ψ\varphi=\mathds{Q}_{1}x_{1}\ldots\mathds{Q}_{n}x_{n}~(\alpha^{1},x_{1})\ldots(\alpha^{n},x_{n}).~\psi be an SL sentence, where each ℚi∈{∃,∀}\mathds{Q}_{i}\in\{\exists,\forall\} for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. Intuitively, our objective is to identify a tuple of best-response functions that select a strategy witness for each ℚi=∃\mathds{Q}_{i}=\exists, such that the probability of induced paths satisfying ψ\psi is maximized. We focus on SL fragments with at most one quantifier alternation (i.e., ∀∗∃∗\forall^{*}\exists^{*} and ∃∗∀∗\exists^{*}\forall^{*}), which capture two mostly common objectives in adversarial RL: learning a response strategy for each opponent strategy and learning a single strategy for the controlled agents that works against all opponent strategies, respectively. These objectives are relevant to games involving two players or two opposing teams, such as Markov soccer Littman (1994), Kuhn poker Kuhn (2016), Predator–Prey, GRF, and SMAC. In addition, the existence of a Nash equilibrium can be expressed in SL using only one quantifier alternation Beutner and Finkbeiner (2024).

We define ℚ∃≜{i∣ℚi=∃}{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}\triangleq\{i\mid\mathds{Q}_{i}=\exists\} and ℚ∀≜{j∣ℚj=∀}{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\forall}}\triangleq\{j\mid\mathds{Q}_{j}=\forall\} as the sets of indices of existentially and universally quantified strategy variables, respectively. Let 𝐏𝐫𝐞≜{j∈ℚ∀∣j<min⁡(ℚ∃)}\mathbf{Pre}\triangleq\{j\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\forall}}\mid j<\min({\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}})\} denote the set of indices of universal quantifiers preceding the first existentially quantified variable. Given a complete strategy assignment 𝒳\mathcal{X}, we define a strategy context Ξ≜⟨𝒳⁡(xj)⟩j∈𝐏𝐫𝐞\Xi\triangleq\langle\mathcal{X}(x_{j})\rangle_{j\in\mathbf{Pre}} as a tuple of strategies assigned to all the preceding universally quantified variables.

We now introduce our key objective. For each i∈ℚ∃i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}, we define a response function 𝐑𝐒xi:Π|𝐏𝐫𝐞|→Π\mathbf{RS}_{x_{i}}:\Pi^{|\mathbf{Pre}|}\rightarrow\Pi, which maps the strategy context Ξ∈Π|𝐏𝐫𝐞|\Xi\in\Pi^{|\mathbf{Pre}|} to a concrete strategy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi. Whenever φ\varphi is of the form ∃∗∀∗\exists^{*}\forall^{*}, then function 𝐑𝐒xi\mathbf{RS}_{x_{i}} becomes a constant function for all i∈ℚ∃i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}, because 𝐏𝐫𝐞={}\mathbf{Pre}=\{\} and Ξ=⟨⟩\Xi=\langle\rangle. Finally, among all possible response functions, we denote the best response function by 𝐁𝐑\mathbf{BR}; i.e., the one that gives optimal probability of satisfying φ\varphi.

Suppose that the strategy space is as follows (where ∗* denotes an arbitrary history prefix):

Π={π1={(e,R),(∗f,D),(∗c,L),(∗b,L)},π3={(b,L),(∗a,U),(∗d,U),(∗g,R),(e,S)},π2={(e,L),(∗d,S),(∗a,R),(∗b,R)},π4={(b,R),(∗c,U),(∗f,U),(∗i,L),(e,S)}}\displaystyle\Pi=\left\{\begin{aligned} \pi_{1}&=\{(e,R),(*f,D),(*c,L),(*b,L)\},~~\pi_{3}=\{(b,L),(*a,U),(*d,U),(*g,R),(e,S)\},\\ \pi_{2}&=\{(e,L),(*d,S),(*a,R),(*b,R)\},~~\pi_{4}=\{(b,R),(*c,U),(*f,U),(*i,L),(e,S)\}\end{aligned}\right\}

Consider a response function 𝐑𝐒y1={(⟨π1⟩,π3),(⟨π2⟩,π3),(⟨π3⟩,\mathbf{RS}_{y}^{1}=\{(\langle\pi_{1}\rangle,\pi_{3}),(\langle\pi_{2}\rangle,\pi_{3}),(\langle\pi_{3}\rangle, π4),(⟨π4⟩,π3)}\pi_{4}),(\langle\pi_{4}\rangle,\pi_{3})\}. Essentially, (⟨π1⟩,π3)(\langle\pi_{1}\rangle,\pi_{3}) means that when the pirate (i.e., xx) is mapped to the π1\pi_{1}, then 𝐑𝐒y1\mathbf{RS}_{y}^{1} maps ship ∃\exists-quantified variable yy to π3\pi_{3} (i.e., as the response strategy of ship against to pirate). The probability of satisfying the inner-LTL formula ψexp\psi_{\text{exp}} using 𝐑𝐒y1\mathbf{RS}_{y}^{1} is computed by considering the following four cases, each corresponding to a complete assignment: Case 1. For (⟨π1⟩,π3)(\langle\pi_{1}\rangle,\pi_{3}), a path sampled from the distribution associated with this assignment is (e,b)→R,L(f,a)→D,U(c,d)→L,U(b,g)→L,R(a,h)(e,b)\xrightarrow{R,L}(f,a)\xrightarrow{D,U}(c,d)\xrightarrow{L,U}(b,g)\xrightarrow{L,R}(a,h), which satisfies the inner-LTL formula (i.e., ⊧ψexp\models\psi_{\text{exp}}). Case 2. For (⟨π2⟩,π3)(\langle\pi_{2}\rangle,\pi_{3}), A path sampled from the distribution associated with this assignment is (e,b)→L,L(d,a)→S,U(d,d)→S,U(d,g)→S,R(d,h)(e,b)\xrightarrow{L,L}(d,a)\xrightarrow{S,U}(d,d)\xrightarrow{S,U}(d,g)\xrightarrow{S,R}(d,h), which does not satisfy the inner-LTL formula (i.e., ⊧̸ψexp\not\models\psi_{\text{exp}}, because ship is intercepted at cell dd). Case 3. Similarly, for (⟨π3⟩,π4)(\langle\pi_{3}\rangle,\pi_{4}), the induced path satisfies the inner-LTL formula. Case 4. Similarly, for (⟨π4⟩,π3)(\langle\pi_{4}\rangle,\pi_{3}), the induced path also satisfies the inner-LTL formula. Hence, the probability of satisfying the SL formula φexp\varphi_{\text{exp}} using 𝐑𝐒y1\mathbf{RS}_{y}^{1} is 0.750.75 .

However, suppose that in the next iteration we identify another response function 𝐑𝐒y2={(⟨π1⟩,π3),(⟨π2⟩,π4),(⟨π3⟩,π4),(⟨π4⟩,π3)}\mathbf{RS}_{y}^{2}=\{(\langle\pi_{1}\rangle,\pi_{3}),(\langle\pi_{2}\rangle,\pi_{4}),(\langle\pi_{3}\rangle,\pi_{4}),(\langle\pi_{4}\rangle,\pi_{3})\}. When the strategy context is ⟨π2⟩\langle\pi_{2}\rangle, 𝐑𝐒y2\mathbf{RS}_{y}^{2} returns π4\pi_{4} for ship, and the induced path satisfies the inner-LTL formula. All remaining I/O in 𝐑𝐒y2\mathbf{RS}_{y}^{2} satisfy φ\varphi with the same analysis as 𝐑𝐒y1\mathbf{RS}_{y}^{1}. Therefore, the probability of satisfying φexp\varphi_{\text{exp}} using 𝐑𝐒y2\mathbf{RS}_{y}^{2} increases to 11 (as it remedies Case 2 which 𝐑𝐒y1\mathbf{RS}_{y}^{1} fails). Hence, 𝐑𝐒y2\mathbf{RS}_{y}^{2} is returned as the best-response function.

5 Algorithmic Details of SLICR

In this section, we describe the algorithmic details of SLICR (see Fig. 2). We first identify the challenges involved in solving the problem formulated in Sec. 4, and then present the components of SLICR designed to address each challenge.

Challenges and Overview of SLICR.

First, recall that our objective in Sec. 4 is to find best-response functions that satisfy an SL specification under its binary semantics. We transform this temporal satisfaction problem into a robustness optimization problem using the quantitative semantics (Sec. 5.1). Second, universally quantified strategy variables may be assigned irrational strategies, resulting in noisy strategy contexts that can mislead the learning agents and degrade their performance. Therefore, SLICR identifies these strategies and prevents the corresponding experiences from affecting the learning process through a shielding mechanism (Sec. 5.2). Third, agents bound by existentially quantified strategy variables must respond to a wide range of strategies assigned to agents bound by preceding universally quantified variables. Thus, each response function takes as input a strategy context, which is a tuple of strategies. Since each strategy is itself a function, this tuple cannot be directly provided as input to a learnable response function. SLICR infers an embedding of the strategy context from the limited observations available to the agent (Sec. 5.3).

5.1 Quantitative Semantics of Inner-LTL Formulas

To obtain an optimization objective for SL satisfaction, we equip the inner-LTL formula with quantitative semantics (Li et al., 2017). Given a complete assignment 𝒳∈𝕏c\mathcal{X}\in\mathbb{X}_{c} and those selected by 𝐑𝐒\mathbf{RS} for agents bound to existentially quantified variables, we sample a path with length TT from the POSG GG and quantitatively evaluate the inner-LTL formula ψ\psi over this path. Let ℝ\mathbb{R} denote the set of real numbers, Ψ\Psi the set of all LTL formulas, and f:2𝖠𝖯→ℝ\mathit{f}:2^{\mathsf{AP}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} a valuation function that assigns a real value to each set of atomic propositions. For a state s∈S\mathit{s}\in S in GG, quantitative semantics are defined by predicates of the form f⁡(L⁡(s))\mathit{f}\big({\mathit{L}(\mathit{s})}\big) (see App. C for full semantics). The robustness function ρ:𝖳𝗋𝖺𝖼𝖾𝗌⁡(𝒵∗)×Ψ→ℝ{\rho}:\mathsf{Traces}(\mathcal{Z}^{*})\times\Psi\rightarrow\mathbb{R} assigns a real-valued robustness value to each finite trace and LTL formula, bounded below by ρ𝑚𝑖𝑛{\rho}_{\mathit{min}} and above by ρ𝑚𝑎𝑥{\rho}_{\mathit{max}}. Formally, given an inner-LTL formula ψ\psi and a POSG GG, we reformulate the problem statement introduced in Sec. 4 as follows:

⟨𝐁𝐑xi⟩i∈ℚ∃∈[arg⁡max⟨𝐑𝐒xi⟩ℙ𝒳∼μ⁡(𝕏c)[ρ(𝖳𝗋((ζ[0:T]∼G𝒳[xi,αi↦𝐑𝐒xi(Ξ)])),ψ)→⋆ρ𝑚𝑎𝑥]]i∈ℚ∃\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{BR}_{x_{i}}\rangle_{i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}}\in\bigg[\underset{\langle\mathbf{RS}_{x_{i}}\rangle}{{\arg\max}}~~\underset{\mathcal{X}\sim\mu(\mathbb{X}_{c})}{\mathbb{P}}\Big[{\rho}\big({\mathsf{Tr}\big((\zeta_{[0:T]}\sim G_{\mathcal{X}[{x_{i}},{\alpha}^{i}\mapsto\mathbf{RS}_{x_{i}}(\Xi)]})\big),\psi}\big)\overset{\star}{\rightarrow}{\rho}_{\mathit{max}}\Big]\bigg]_{i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}} (2)

where →⋆\overset{\star}{\rightarrow} denotes convergence. That is, the tuple of best-response functions ⟨𝐁𝐑xi⟩i∈ℚ∃\langle\mathbf{BR}_{x_{i}}\rangle_{i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}} maximizes the probability that the robustness of a path sampled from GG under the complete assignment 𝒳\mathcal{X} converges to ρ𝑚𝑎𝑥{\rho}_{\mathit{max}}, thereby optimizing the satisfiability of the inner-LTL formula ψ\psi.

5.2 Shielding from Noisy Strategies

We define an irrational strategy as an observation-independent strategy that selects actions uniformly at random. 5.3 Learning Best-Response Functions

We now address the optimization problem in Eq. 2. Our learning framework follows the Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm (Oliehoek et al., 2016). Conceptually, during centralized training, agents bound to existentially quantified variables have access to observations and actions of agents bound to preceding universally quantified variables. During execution, each agent has access only to its local information.

Robustness Values as Reward Signals.

To solve Eq. 2, we derive reward signals that guide the learning of response functions. Given a 𝒳∈𝕏c\mathcal{X}\in\mathbb{X}_{c}, the reward for each αi{\alpha}^{i}, where i∈ℚ∃i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}, at step kk is computed as ρ(𝖳𝗋((ζ∼G𝒳)[0:k+1]),ψ){\rho}\big({\mathsf{Tr}\big((\zeta\sim G_{\mathcal{X}})_{[0:k+1]}\big),\psi}\big). Given a discount factor γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1), we learn best-response functions that maximize the expected cumulative discounted robustness:

⟨𝐁𝐑xi⟩i∈ℚ∃∈[arg⁡max⟨𝐑𝐒xi⟩𝔼𝒳∼μ⁡(𝕏c)ζ∼G𝒳[xi,αi↦𝐑𝐒xi(Ξ)][∑k=0T−1γkρ(𝖳𝗋(ζ[0:k+1]),ψ)]]i∈ℚ∃\langle\mathbf{BR}_{x_{i}}\rangle_{i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}}\in\bigg[\underset{\langle\mathbf{RS}_{x_{i}}\rangle}{\arg\max}\;\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{X}\sim\mu(\mathbb{X}_{c})\\ \zeta\sim G_{\mathcal{X}[x_{i},{\alpha}^{i}\mapsto\mathbf{RS}_{x_{i}}(\Xi)]}\end{subarray}}{\mathbb{E}}\bigg[\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\gamma^{k}{\rho}\big({\mathsf{Tr}\big(\zeta_{[0:k+1]}\big),\psi}\big)\bigg]\bigg]_{i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}} (3)

Note that, in this setting, reward signals are derived from the inner-LTL formula, so all existentially quantified agents receive the same reward. However, more generally, a POSG may assign distinct rewards to individual agents. We can capture this setting by decomposing ψ\psi into agent-specific subformulas, ψ=⋀i∈ℚ∃ψi\psi=\bigwedge_{i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}}\psi_{i}, where each ψi\psi_{i} represents an objective or constraint associated with an agent αi{\alpha}^{i}. The reward for agent αi{\alpha}^{i} at step kk is then individually computed as ρ(𝖳𝗋((ζ∼G𝒳)[0:k+1]),ψi){\rho}\big({\mathsf{Tr}\big((\zeta\sim G_{\mathcal{X}})_{[0:k+1]}\big),\psi_{i}}\big). For simplicity, we present the remainder of our algorithm using a single full inner-LTL formula ψ\psi.

Representing Strategy Context.

As shown in Eq. 3, for each i∈ℚ∃i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}, the response function 𝐑𝐒xi\mathbf{RS}_{x_{i}} takes Ξ\Xi as an input. This raises two difficulties. First, Ξ∈Π|𝐏𝐫𝐞|\Xi\in\Pi^{|\mathbf{Pre}|} is a |𝐏𝐫𝐞||\mathbf{Pre}|-tuple of strategies, each of which is itself a function. Therefore, providing this tuple as input to a learnable response function requires a suitable finite-dimensional representation. Second, due to the partial observability of the POSG, each agent αi{\alpha}^{i}, where i∈ℚ∃i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}, must infer this representation from its local history hαi∈ℋ∗h_{{\alpha}^{i}}\in\mathcal{H}^{*}. We associate the strategy-context space Π|𝐏𝐫𝐞|\Pi^{|\mathbf{Pre}|} with a latent context space Λ⊆ℝd\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}, where d∈ℤ>0d\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} denotes the dimension of the latent context embedding. Let λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda denote a latent embedding. We call λ\lambda an information-preserving latent context embedding of Ξ\Xi (denoted λΞ\lambda_{\Xi}), if it represents Ξ\Xi without information loss, meaning that Ξ\Xi can be uniquely recovered from λ\lambda.

We are inspired by the agent-modeling approach proposed in (Papoudakis et al., 2021a), which uses an encoder-decoder architecture to learn embeddings of other agents from the controlled agent’s local information under partial observability. We define encoder Ew:ℋ∗→ΛE_{w}:\mathcal{H}^{*}\rightarrow\Lambda, parameterized by ww, that maps the history hαi∈ℋ∗h_{{\alpha}^{i}}\in\mathcal{H}^{*} of any agent αi{\alpha}^{i}, where i∈ℚ∃i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}, to a latent embedding λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda. Next, we define two decoders: an action-reconstruction decoder 𝐷𝐴w​a:Λ→Δ​(A)|𝐏𝐫𝐞|\mathit{DA}_{wa}:\Lambda\rightarrow\Delta(A)^{|\mathbf{Pre}|}, and an observation-reconstruction 𝐷𝑂w​o:Λ→O|𝐏𝐫𝐞|\mathit{DO}_{wo}:\Lambda\rightarrow\mathit{O}^{|\mathbf{Pre}|}, parameterized by w​awa and w​owo, respectively. These decoders map a latent embedding λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda to the reconstructed actions and observations of agents bound to the preceding universally quantified variables, respectively. In addition, we use the latent embedding to predict their actions over the next LL-steps. This prediction encourages the latent embedding to capture information about their future behavior. Formally, we define a future-action predictor F𝑤𝑓:Λ→Δ​(A)|𝐏𝐫𝐞|×LF_{\mathit{wf}}:\Lambda\rightarrow\Delta(A)^{|\mathbf{Pre}|\times L}, parameterized by 𝑤𝑓\mathit{wf}, where L∈ℤ>0L\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} denotes the prediction window. Further details on computing the latent embedding are provided in Sec. D.2.

Learning Response Functions.

Recall that, as defined in Secs. 3 and 4, each complete assignment 𝒳∈𝕏c\mathcal{X}\in\mathbb{X}_{c} induces a distribution G𝒳G_{\mathcal{X}} over finite paths, from which a path ζ∼G𝒳\zeta\sim G_{\mathcal{X}} is sampled. For each i∈ℚ∃i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}, we seek a 𝐑𝐒xi\mathbf{RS}_{x_{i}} that maximizes the objective in Eq. 3. Given a Ξ\Xi, the 𝐑𝐒xi​(Ξ)\mathbf{RS}_{x_{i}}(\Xi) returns a strategy for variable xix_{i} and agent αi{\alpha}^{i}, where each strategy is a mapping π:ℋ∗→Δ⁡(A)\pi:\mathcal{H}^{*}\rightarrow\Delta(A). Hence, assigning a strategy π\pi alone does not determine its action distribution during sampling, as π\pi depends on the history observed by αi{\alpha}^{i}. As described earlier, we use the latent embedding λΞ\lambda_{\Xi} to represent the strategy context Ξ\Xi. Hence, to explicitly represent how the assigned strategies generate actions during learning, we define its equivalent action-level response function 𝐑𝐒xia:Λ×ℋ∗→Δ⁡(A)\mathbf{RS}^{a}_{x_{i}}:\Lambda\times\mathcal{H}^{*}\rightarrow\Delta(A), which maps a latent embedding and a history to a distribution over the actions.

Now, let ⟨ai⟩i∈I\langle\mathit{a}_{i}\rangle_{i\in I} and ⟨aj⟩j∈J\langle\mathit{a}_{j}\rangle_{j\in J} be two action tuples, where I∪J={1,…,n}I\cup J=\{1,\ldots,n\} and I∩J=∅I\cap J=\emptyset. To combine these tuples while preserving the order according to their indices, we use the operator ⊕\oplus, which returns a single tuple ordered by index. Given a complete assignment 𝒳∈𝕏c\mathcal{X}\in\mathbb{X}_{c} and a tuple of action-level response functions ⟨𝐑𝐒xia⟩i∈ℚ∃\langle\mathbf{RS}^{a}_{x_{i}}\rangle_{i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}}, a joint action 𝐚\mathbf{a} at step kk is defined as:

6 Experiments and Results

Our experiments target the maximization problem in Eq. 4. Its connection to the objective in Eq. 1 is established theoretically through Theorem 5.3 and Lemmas 5.2 and 5.1, with the resulting guarantees conditional on their stated assumptions.

Implementation Pipeline.

We first construct Π\Pi using off-the-shelf MARL algorithms, including IPPO and MAPPO (Yu et al., 2022), VDN (Sunehag et al., 2017),QMIX (Rashid et al., 2018), and QTRAN (Son et al., 2019), together with irrational strategies that select actions uniformly at random. Let ΠTrain\Pi^{\text{Train}} and ΠTest\Pi^{\text{Test}} denote the strategy sets used during training and evaluation, respectively. We evaluate performance in two settings: (1) Seen, where ΠTrain=ΠTest\Pi^{\text{Train}}=\Pi^{\text{Test}}, and (2) Unseen, where ΠTrain∩ΠTest=∅\Pi^{\text{Train}}\cap\Pi^{\text{Test}}=\emptyset. During training phase, we use the quantitative semantics (Sec. 5.1) to compute robustness-based rewards from the SL formula. For each i∈ℚ∃i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}, we then train the response function using hαih_{{\alpha}^{i}} and λ\lambda with A2C, PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) or IPPO, while the pretrained   \mathord{\lx@scalerel@obj{\hbox to9.12pt{\vbox to13.26pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.25555pt\lower-2.96805pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{ {}{{}}{}{{}}{}{{}}{}{}{} {}{}{{}}{}{{}}{}{}{}{{}}{}{{}}{}{}{} {}{}{{}}{}{{}}{}{}{} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=1.2pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@roundcap\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-linecap=round} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@roundjoin\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-linejoin=round} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 5.96 13.4 C 4.29 11.92 2.26 10.6 0.48 10.6 L 0.48 5.06 C 0.48 0.89 2.68 -2.26 5.96 -3.28 C 9.23 -2.26 11.44 0.89 11.44 5.06 L 11.44 10.6 C 9.65 10.6 7.63 11.92 5.96 13.4 Z}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces \lxSVG@closescope } \lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}} excludes experiences associated with irrational strategies. We report results over ten independent runs with different random seeds. Further experimental and implementation details are provided in App. D.

Benchmarks.

We evaluate SLICR on three benchmarks. (1) Predator and Prey (PP) (Lowe et al., 2017). We use the implementation provided by (Papoudakis et al., 2021a). PP consists of one existentially quantified prey that must be captured by exactly one of three universally quantified predators. We adopt the strategy sets from (Papoudakis et al., 2021b) and develop novel, diverse IPPO, MAPPO, and irrational predator strategies. (2) Google Research Football (GRF) (Kurach et al., 2020). We evaluate two scenarios. First, in “Run to Score” (R2S), a player (bound to an existentially quantified variable) starts at the midfield and must score against a goalkeeper while five opposing players (bound to universally quantified variables) are chasing from behind. Second, in “Run to Score with two Defenders” (R2S-DEF), inspired by (Odrowaz-Sypniewski et al., 2026), two of the opposing players are positioned between the existentially quantified player and the goal, while the remaining three are chasing from behind. Third, in “Run to Score with four Defenders” (R2S-4DEF), where four of the opposing players are positioned between the existentially quantified player and the goal, while the one remaining is chasing from behind. To construct a diverse strategy set, we train IPPO, MAPPO, and built-in AI opponent teams with different tactical behaviors. (3) SMAC-HARD (Deng et al., 2024). We evaluated our extension with pretrained MARL opponent populations on three maps: 3m, 2s3z, and 3s_vs_3z. The objective of the existentially quantified agents is to eliminate all universally quantified agents. To construct a diverse strategies set, we use VDN, QMIX, QTRAN, and built-in AI opponents. Further details on the environment settings, SL formulas, and opponent strategies are provided in App. E.

Experimental Organization.

We assess SLICR along four dimensions: (1) Comparing SLICR with LIAM (Papoudakis et al., 2021a), an opponent-modeling baseline for partially observable environments. (2) Comparing the ∀∗∃∗\forall^{*}\exists^{*} and ∃∗∀∗\exists^{*}\forall^{*} fragments of the target SL formulas in terms of effectiveness and parameter efficiency. (3) Comparing SLICR and LIAM in the presence of irrational strategies. (4) Investigating how the inner-LTL formula guides and improves learning.

(1) SLICR vs. LIAM.

Since SLICR represents strategy context as a latent embedding, we compare it with LIAM, an opponent-modeling method for partially observable settings. Both methods use A2C on PP and PPO on GRF and SMAC-HARD. In PP (see Fig. 6), SLICR achieves up to ↑400{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt400} and ↑200{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt200} more single-predator collisions than LIAM over 100 evaluation episodes in the Seen and Unseen settings, respectively.

On the more complex GRF benchmark, SLICR significantly outperforms LIAM. In R2S (see Fig. 3(a)), SLICR surpasses LIAM after 2M training steps and ultimately scores ↑30{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt30} and ↑20{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt20} more goals over 100 evaluation episodes in the Seen and Unseen settings, respectively. Similarly, in the R2S-DEF scenario (see Fig. 3(b)), SLICR outperforms LIAM, scoring up to ↑30{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt30} and ↑35{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt35} more goals in the Seen and Unseen settings, respectively. In addition, in the harder R2S-4DEF scenario (see Fig. 3(c)), SLICR outperforms LIAM, scoring up to ↑10{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt10} more goals in the Seen and Unseen settings.

The superiority of SLICR extends to the SMAC-HARD as well. On 3m (see Fig. 3(d)), SLICR achieves up to ↑25%{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt25\%} and ↑15%{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt15\%} higher win rates than LIAM in the Seen and Unseen settings, respectively. In the Seen setting, SLICR reaches ≈\approx100%100\% win rate after 400K steps, whereas LIAM does not within the 500K-step training budget. On 2s3z (see Fig. 3(e)), SLICR reaches ≈\approx95%95\% win rate after 400K steps, outperforming LIAM by up to ↑30%{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt30\%} and ↑20%{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt20\%} in the Seen and Unseen settings, respectively. The performance of SLICR is particularly substantial on 3s_vs_3z (see Fig. 3(f)). In the Seen setting, SLICR reaches a 100%100\% win rate after ≈\approx700K steps, while LIAM reaches only ≈\approx40%40\% within the 1M-step training, yielding a gain of ↑60%{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt60\%}. In the Unseen setting, SLICR achieves ≈\approx90%90\% win rate, whereas LIAM rarely wins, yielding a gain up to ↑90%{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt90\%}.

We also investigate decentralized learning of action-level best responses in SMAC-HARD using IPPO, since it is the only benchmark with multiple controlled agents (agents bound to existentially quantified variables). On the 3m map (see Fig. 3(g)), we observe that in the Seen setting, SLICR converges to a 100%100\% win rate after ≈\approx400400K training steps, while LIAM achieves ≈\approx80%80\% after 400K training steps. On the 2s3z map (see Fig. 3(h)), SLICR performs slightly better than LIAM in both the Seen and Unseen settings. On 3s_vs_3z (see Fig. 3(i)), similar to the PPO setting, SLICR performs substantially better in both the Seen and Unseen settings. In the Seen setting, SLICR achieves a 100%100\% win rate after ≈\approx700700K steps, while LIAM reaches only ≈\approx60%60\% within the 1M-step training budget, yielding a gain of ↑40%{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt40}\% points. In the Unseen setting, SLICR achieves a win rate of ≈\approx80%80\%, whereas LIAM achieves ≈\approx10%10\%, yielding a gain of up to ↑70%{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt70}\% points. Further results are in App. F.1.

(2) SLICR ∀∗∃∗\bm{\forall^{*}\exists^{*}} vs. ∃∗∀∗\bm{\exists^{*}\forall^{*}}.

These two SL fragments induce different learning pipelines. Under ∀∗∃∗\forall^{*}\exists^{*}, each response function is conditioned on the agent’s history and latent embedding (i.e. strategy context) of the preceding universal agents’ strategies, whereas under ∃∗∀∗\exists^{*}\forall^{*}, it uses only the local information. Consequently, the former is more parameter-intensive, as quantified across benchmarks in Table 1. This is expected because solving the ∀∗∃∗\forall^{*}\exists^{*} problem is generally harder; however, it yields adaptive strategies. However, SLICR (∀∗∃∗\forall^{*}\exists^{*}) outperforms SLICR (∃∗∀∗\exists^{*}\forall^{*}) by up to ↑526{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt526} and ↑380{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt380} in the Seen and Unseen settings, respectively. This improvement is particularly substantial in the GRF scenarios. In R2S, SLICR (∀∗∃∗\forall^{*}\exists^{*}) achieves approximately ×4\times 4 and ×3\times 3 scores in the Seen and Unseen settings, respectively. Similarly, in R2S-DEF, it achieves approximately ×1.5\times 1.5 and ×4\times 4 scores, respectively. In contrast, in the SMAC-HARD scenarios, (∀∗∃∗\forall^{*}\exists^{*}) and (∃∗∀∗\exists^{*}\forall^{*}) perform similarly, although (∀∗∃∗\forall^{*}\exists^{*}) performs slightly better in 4/6 cases. This suggests that the heavier (∀∗∃∗\forall^{*}\exists^{*}) pipeline is not necessary for all cases, and (∃∗∀∗\exists^{*}\forall^{*}) can be sufficient. Additional analysis is provided in App. F.2.

(3) SLICR vs. LIAM Under Irrational Strategies

Fig. 4 shows how the shield   \mathord{\lx@scalerel@obj{\hbox to9.12pt{\vbox to13.26pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.25555pt\lower-2.96805pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{ {}{{}}{}{{}}{}{{}}{}{}{} {}{}{{}}{}{{}}{}{}{}{{}}{}{{}}{}{}{} {}{}{{}}{}{{}}{}{}{} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=1.2pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@roundcap\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-linecap=round} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@roundjoin\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-linejoin=round} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 5.96 13.4 C 4.29 11.92 2.26 10.6 0.48 10.6 L 0.48 5.06 C 0.48 0.89 2.68 -2.26 5.96 -3.28 C 9.23 -2.26 11.44 0.89 11.44 5.06 L 11.44 10.6 C 9.65 10.6 7.63 11.92 5.96 13.4 Z}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces \lxSVG@closescope } \lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}} protects SLICR when ΠTrain\Pi^{\text{Train}} contains irrational strategies. Across settings containing 20%20\%, 30%30\%, 40%40\%, or 50%50\% irrational strategies, SLICR (solid lines) achieves up to ↑300{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt300} more single-predator collisions than LIAM (corresponding dashed lines). A shield ablation study is provided in App. F.3.

(4) Inner-LTL vs. Shaped Reward.

Fig. 5 compares inner-LTL guidance with shaped rewards. On GRF R2S-DEF (left), guidance from φR2S-DEF\varphi_{\text{R2S-DEF}} enables SLICR to achieve up to ↑15{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt15} and ↑20{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt20} more goals in the Seen (blue line) and Unseen (orange line) settings, respectively. On 3s_vs_3z (right), guidance from φSMAC\varphi_{\text{SMAC}} improves the win rate by up to ↑30%{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt30\%} in Seen and ↑35%{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt35\%} in Unseen. In Seen, both variants eventually approach a 100%100\% win rate, resulting in similar behavior at the end of training, while Unseen gain persists throughout. Additional ablations are provided in App. F.4.

7 Conclusion

SLICR is a specification-guided MARL framework for partially observable adversarial settings. By employing Strategic Logic, SLICR explicitly reasons about agents’ strategies and their responses to adversaries. Our evaluation on Predator-Prey, Google Research Football, and SMAC-HARD demonstrates that SLICR is effective, scalable, and adaptable across adversarial strategies, improving opponent-modeling baselines by up to 90%{90\%}.

Limitations.

SLICR is limited to SL fragments with at most one quantifier alternation, which we believe are sufficient to express many adversarial RL problems. Also, its theoretical guarantees rely on information-preserving latent embedding, which may be hard to achieve under partial observability. The information-preserving latent embedding condition directly concerns the opponent-strategy information available to SLICR in practice. The remaining assumptions are not prerequisites for executing SLICR, whose practical objective is to learn action-level best-response functions that maximize Eq. 4. These assumptions support the theoretical guarantees connecting this optimization objective to the maximization of satisfaction probability in Eq. 1 of Sec. 4.

Appendix B Proofs

B.1 Proof of Lemma 5.1

Proof 1

We assume that the convergence objective is order-preserving with respect to satisfaction, meaning that a tuple of response functions with a higher probability of convergence to the maximum robustness value cannot have a lower probability of satisfying the specification. We now begin the proof by let, 𝔅=⟨𝐁𝐑xi⟩i∈ℚ∃\mathfrak{B}=\langle\mathbf{BR}_{x_{i}}\rangle_{i\in{\mathds{\mathds{Q}}^{\exists}}} be a tuple of best-response functions that maximizes Eq. 2, and let 𝖳𝗋⁡(ζ𝒳𝔅)\mathsf{Tr}(\zeta_{\mathcal{X}}^{\mathfrak{B}}) denote a trace sampled under a complete assignment 𝒳\mathcal{X} updated by a tuple 𝔅\mathfrak{B}.

Since ρ𝑚𝑎𝑥{\rho}_{\mathit{max}} is the greatest positive robustness value, convergence to ρ𝑚𝑎𝑥{\rho}_{\mathit{max}} implies positive robustness. By the soundness of the quantitative semantics Li et al. (2017), positive robustness implies satisfaction. Therefore,

ρ⁡(𝖳𝗋⁡(ζ𝒳𝔅),ψ)→∗ρ𝑚𝑎𝑥⟹ρ⁡(𝖳𝗋⁡(ζ𝒳𝔅),ψ)>0⟹𝖳𝗋⁡(ζ𝒳𝔅)⊧ψ.{\rho}\big({\mathsf{Tr}(\zeta_{\mathcal{X}}^{\mathfrak{B}}),\psi}\big)\xrightarrow{*}{\rho}_{\mathit{max}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad{\rho}\big({\mathsf{Tr}(\zeta_{\mathcal{X}}^{\mathfrak{B}}),\psi}\big)>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathsf{Tr}(\zeta_{\mathcal{X}}^{\mathfrak{B}})\models\psi.

Thus, convergence to ρ𝑚𝑎𝑥{\rho}_{\mathit{max}} guarantees satisfaction of ψ\psi. By the order-preservation assumption, a tuple with a higher probability of convergence cannot have a lower probability of satisfaction. Since 𝔅\mathfrak{B} maximizes the probability of convergence in Eq. 2, it also maximizes the probability of satisfying ψ\psi. Hence, maximizing this satisfaction probability is exactly the optimization problem stated in Sec. 4. Therefore, 𝔅\mathfrak{B} also solves the original optimization problem.

B.2 Proof of Lemma 5.2

Proof 2

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} denote the set of well-typed response-function tuples, and let J2,J3:ℬ→ℝJ_{2},J_{3}:\mathcal{B}\to\mathbb{R} denote the objectives in Eq. 2 and  Eq. 3, respectively. By assumption, J3J_{3} strictly preserves the ordering induced by J2J_{2}; that is, for any 𝐁,𝐁′∈ℬ\mathbf{B},\mathbf{B}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}, we have:

J2​(𝐁)>J2​(𝐁′)⟹J3​(𝐁)>J3​(𝐁′).J_{2}(\mathbf{B})>J_{2}(\mathbf{B}^{\prime})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad J_{3}(\mathbf{B})>J_{3}(\mathbf{B}^{\prime}).

Let 𝐁∗∈arg⁡max𝐁∈ℬ​J3​(𝐁)\mathbf{B}^{*}\in\arg\max\limits_{\mathbf{B}\in\mathcal{B}}J_{3}(\mathbf{B}). Suppose, for contradiction, that 𝐁∗\mathbf{B}^{*} does not maximize J2J_{2}. Then there exists some 𝐁^∈ℬ\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\in\mathcal{B} such that:

J2​(𝐁^)>J2​(𝐁∗).J_{2}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}})>J_{2}(\mathbf{B}^{*}).

By strict order preservation, this implies:

J3​(𝐁^)>J3​(𝐁∗),J_{3}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}})>J_{3}(\mathbf{B}^{*}),

which contradicts the assumption that 𝐁∗\mathbf{B}^{*} maximizes J3J_{3}. Therefore,

arg⁡max𝐁∈ℬ​J3​(𝐁)⊆arg⁡max𝐁∈ℬ​J2​(𝐁);\arg\max_{\mathbf{B}\in\mathcal{B}}J_{3}(\mathbf{B})\subseteq\arg\max_{\mathbf{B}\in\mathcal{B}}J_{2}(\mathbf{B});

hence, every maximizer of Eq. 3 also maximizes Eq. 2.

B.3 Proof of Theorem 5.3

Proof 3

Let us write:

𝔅a=⟨𝐁𝐑xia⟩i∈ℚ∃\mathfrak{B}^{a}=\langle\mathbf{BR}_{x_{i}}^{a}\rangle_{i\in\mathbb{Q}^{\exists}}

as a tuple of action-level best-response functions maximizing the expected cumulative discounted robustness value. Since λΞ\lambda_{\Xi} is information-preserving for every strategy context Ξ\Xi, the latent representation retains all information required by a well-typed best-response function. Hence, for every 𝐁𝐑xia\mathbf{BR}_{x_{i}}^{a} in the optimal tuple 𝔅a\mathfrak{B}^{a}, there exists an induced best-response function 𝐁𝐑xi\mathbf{BR}_{x_{i}} on the original strategy context, such that:

𝐁𝐑xi​(Ξ)​(h)=𝐁𝐑xia​(λΞ,h),\mathbf{BR}_{x_{i}}(\Xi)(\mathit{h})=\mathbf{BR}_{x_{i}}^{a}(\lambda_{\Xi},\mathit{h}),

and the two functions induce the same action choices given the same history h\mathit{h}, and therefore the same distribution over trajectories. Consequently, for every complete assignment 𝒳∈𝕏c\mathcal{X}\in\mathbb{X}_{c}, the trajectory distribution induced by 𝔅a\mathfrak{B}^{a} in the latent representation coincides with that induced by the corresponding best-response function tuple:

𝔅=⟨𝐁𝐑xi⟩i∈ℚ∃\mathfrak{B}=\langle\mathbf{BR}_{x_{i}}\rangle_{i\in\mathbb{Q}^{\exists}}

in the original representation. In particular, their expected cumulative discounted robustness values are equal:

Ja​(𝔅a)=J3​(𝔅),J_{a}(\mathfrak{B}^{a})=J_{3}(\mathfrak{B}),

where JaJ_{a} denotes the action-level objective defined immediately before Theorem 5.3 and J3J_{3} denotes the objective in Eq. 3.

Because the embedding is information-preserving and the action-level response functions can represent every well-typed response function, every well-typed response tuple has an equivalent action-level tuple that induces the same trajectory distribution and objective value. Therefore, if 𝔅a\mathfrak{B}^{a} maximizes JaJ_{a}, the induced tuple 𝔅\mathfrak{B} maximizes J3J_{3}; otherwise, a well-typed tuple with a strictly larger value of J3J_{3} would induce a latent-level response tuple with a strictly larger value of JaJ_{a}, contradicting the optimality of 𝔅a\mathfrak{B}^{a}.

Thus,

𝔅∈arg⁡max𝔅∈ℬ⁡J3.\mathfrak{B}\in\arg\max_{\mathfrak{B}\in\mathcal{B}}J_{3}.

By Lemma 5.2, every maximizer of Eq. 3 also maximizes the objective in Eq. 2. Hence,

𝔅∈arg⁡max𝔅∈ℬ⁡J2.\mathfrak{B}\in\arg\max_{\mathfrak{B}\in\mathcal{B}}J_{2}.

Finally, by Lemma 5.1, every maximizer of Eq. 2 solves the optimization problem of Sec. 4 (i.e., it maximizes the probability of satisfying the SL sentence ψ\psi in GG). Therefore, any tuple of optimal latent-level best-response functions 𝔅a\mathfrak{B}^{a} induces a tuple 𝔅\mathfrak{B} that solves the original satisfaction-probability optimization problem formalized in Eq. 1.

Appendix D Experimental Setup and Implementation Details

In this section, we describe the implementation details, architectures, hyperparameters, and loss functions of the models used in our experiments.

D.1 Details on Shield

We train a recurrent binary classifier to distinguish rational predator (agent bound to universally quantified variable) compositions from irrational tasks. At each time step, the classifier receives the prey’s (agent bound to existentially quantified variable) current observation concatenated with its five previous actions. The previous action vector is zero at the beginning of each interaction sequence. The architecture consists of a single-layer LSTM with 128 hidden units, followed by a fully connected layer with 64 units, a ReLU activation, and a scalar output layer. The recurrent hidden and cell states are reset independently for each interaction sequence.

Data are collected using a uniform-random prey strategy across m=20m=20 training tasks, comprising of ten rational and ten irrational tasks. For each task, we collect 1,000 training interaction sequences and 200 independent calibration interaction sequences, each lasting 20 steps. Ten interaction sequences from the same task form a training bundle. Their final-step logits are averaged before applying a sigmoid to obtain the bundle’s classification score. The classifier is trained using standard class-weighted binary cross-entropy; the balanced dataset gives equal weights to both classes. Interaction sequence are randomly regrouped within each task at every epoch, and the resulting bundles are shuffled. Training runs for 100 epochs using Adam with a learning rate of 0.001, minibatches of 64 bundles, and gradient-norm clipping at 1.0.

Shield in Deployment.

During deployment (main training phase), each collected trajectory receives the stored classification of its opponent task. Experience classified as random is excluded from the actor, critic, and opponent-model losses, while the remaining losses are averaged over retained experience; if none remains in a batch, we skip the update.

D.2 Details on Encoder, Decoders and Future-Action Prediction

Encoder (EE).

SLICR uses a recurrent encoder to summarize the action-observation history of each agent bound to an existentially quantified variable into a latent context representation. At each time step, the encoder receives the agent’s current local observation concatenated with its previous one-hot-encoded action. The encoder consists of a single-layer LSTM with 128 hidden units, followed by a fully connected layer with 128 units and a ReLU activation. A final linear layer produces a 32-dimensional (d=32d=32) embedding without an output activation.

Training uses five-step sequences with truncated backpropagation through time, storing the exact recurrent states at each sequence’s start for replay. The encoder is optimized using Adam with a fixed learning rate of 0.0007 and gradient-norm clipping at 0.5.

Action-Reconstruction Decoder (𝐷𝐴\mathit{DA}).

The action-reconstruction decoder predicts the current action of each agent bound to a preceding universally quantified variable from the encoder’s latent context embedding (λ∈Λ⊆ℝ32\lambda\in\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{32}). It uses a shared feed-forward network with two fully connected hidden layers of 128 units, each followed by a ReLU activation. Separate linear outputs produce action logits for each agent bound to a preceding universally quantified variable, and a softmax converts these logits into categorical action probabilities. This decoder is trained jointly with the encoder using Adam with a learning rate of 0.0007 and gradient-norm clipping at 0.5.

Observation-Reconstruction Decoder (𝐷𝑂\mathit{DO}).

The observation-reconstruction decoder predicts the agents bound to a preceding universally quantified variable observations from the encoder’s latent context embedding (λ∈Λ⊆ℝ32\lambda\in\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{32}). It consists of two fully connected hidden layers with 128 units each, followed by ReLU activations, and a final linear layer that outputs the reconstructed observation vector without an output activation. This branch has separate parameters from the action-reconstruction branch. It is trained jointly with the encoder using Adam with a learning rate of 0.0007 and gradient-norm clipping at 0.5.

Future-Action Predictor (FF).

The future-action predictor estimates each agent bound to a preceding universally quantified variable action distribution over the next 5 steps from the encoder’s latent embedding. It consists of two fully connected hidden layers with 128 units each and ReLU activations, followed by a linear output layer. The output is organized by prediction horizon and an agent bound to a preceding universally quantified variable, with a softmax producing a categorical action for each combination. The predictor is trained jointly with the encoder using Adam with a learning rate of 0.0007 and gradient-norm clipping at 0.5.

Training.

We jointly train the encoder (EE), observation-reconstruction decoder (𝐷𝑂\mathit{DO}), action-reconstruction decoder (𝐷𝐴\mathit{DA}), and future-action predictor (FF) using samples collected. Samples are divided into five-step sequences, and the encoder is replayed from its stored hidden and cell states. Its latent embedding at each step is shared by all three prediction branches. Observation reconstruction (𝐷𝑂w​o\mathit{DO}_{wo}) uses a standard squared-error loss. We sum the squared differences between predicted and recorded observation features, multiply by 0.5, and average over retained steps and environments. Action reconstruction (𝐷𝐴w​a\mathit{DA}_{wa}) uses standard categorical cross-entropy against the opponents’ recorded actions. The losses are summed across opponents and averaged over retained steps and environments. Future-action predictor (Fw​fF_{wf}) uses standard categorical cross-entropy against recorded future actions. The loss is averaged over steps, environments, agents bound to a preceding universally quantified variables , and the five prediction horizons. Targets beyond the available rollout or across episode boundaries are excluded.

The combined loss for learning the latent context embedding is calculated as follows:

ℒλ=ℒ𝐷𝑂+ℒ𝐷𝐴+0.1​ℒF.\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{DO}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{DA}}+0.1\,\mathcal{L}_{F}.

Gradients from all three terms update the shared encoder, while each prediction branch is updated through its own term. We use a shared Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.0007, clipping gradient norms to 0.5 separately for the encoder, decoders, and future-action predictor. Backpropagation is truncated at five-step boundaries, while recurrent states carry information across sequences.

Information-preserving latent context embedding

Let w∗w^{*} denote the encoder parameters obtained by minimizing the combined loss ℒλ\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}. The resulting embedding is λ^=Ew⋆​(hαi)\widehat{\lambda}=E_{w^{\star}}(h_{{\alpha}^{i}}). By jointly reconstructing current actions and observations and predicting future actions, the encoder is encouraged to preserve the information needed to approximate λ\lambda. However, because the encoder has access only to the agent’s local action-observation history, different strategy contexts may be observationally indistinguishable. Therefore, the learned embedding may only approximate the information-preserving latent context embedding.

D.3 Details on Training the Action-level Response Functions

Predator-Prey.

SLICR uses A2C algorithm with a single-layer LSTM containing 128 hidden units. The LSTM processes the current observation and previous one-hot action. Its output is concatenated with the current observation and corrected 32-dimensional latent embedding, producing a 174-dimensional input to the actor and critic. Each network contains two independent fully connected hidden layers with 128 units and ReLU activations. The actor produces a categorical distribution over five actions, while the critic produces a scalar value estimate.

GRF.

SLICR uses a recurrent PPO algorithm with a 128-unit LSTM. The current observation, 32-dimensional latent embedding, and history output form a 275-dimensional input to the actor and critic. Each network contains three independent fully connected hidden layers with 256 units and ReLU activations. The actor produces a categorical distribution over 19 actions, and the critic produces a scalar value estimate. PPO performs five optimization epochs per rollout update, using a clipping threshold of 0.2 for both the probability ratio and value prediction.

SMAC-HARD.

SLICR uses a 128-unit policy LSTM and separate actor and critic networks, each with three 256-unit ReLU hidden layers. Each controlled unit receives its own local observation, previous action, and locally computed latent embedding. Under PPO, response-function parameters are shared across controlled units. Under IPPO, each unit has independent policy LSTM, actor, critic, and future-action-adapter parameters, with its own Adam optimizer; the auxiliary encoder and prediction heads remain shared. In both cases, recurrent hidden and cell states are maintained separately for each unit. Observation and action dimensions depend on the map. Unavailable actions are masked before constructing the categorical action distribution. Both PPO and IPPO use five optimization epochs and clipping thresholds of 0.2 for the probability ratio and value updates.

Training.

Across all three benchmarks, the actor and critic share a policy LSTM, which remains separate from EE. Training uses five-step recurrent sequences for A2C and PPO, and 20-step sequences for IPPO. Hidden and cell states are carried across sequences and reset at episode boundaries. The response function’s learning rate remains constant for the first 30% of training and then decreases linearly to one-tenth of its initial value. For both PPO and IPPO, behavior log probabilities, behavior value estimates, and advantages are fixed before optimization begins; recurrent chunks are shuffled between epochs while timestep order within each chunk is preserved. For IPPO, advantages are normalized separately for each controlled unit, and each unit’s policy parameters are updated using an independent Adam optimizer with gradient-norm clipping applied separately per unit. Details on the hyperparameters for training the response functions appear in Table 2.

Appendix E Benchmark Details

E.1 Predator and Prey

Environment.

We used (Papoudakis et al., 2021a) implementation of predator and prey. The predator–prey environment is a two-dimensional arena containing one prey, three predators, and two stationary obstacles. All agents choose among five discrete actions: {S​t​a​y,l​e​f​t,r​i​g​h​t,U​p,D​o​w​n}\{Stay,left,right,Up,Down\}. Episodes terminate after 50 steps. The prey has partial observation. It observes its own position and velocity, together with the relative positions of obstacles and predators within visible range.

step of each prefix. Because we evaluate the robustness of every prefix throughout an episode, this condition rewards repeated occurrences of contact with exactly one predator.

Learning set of Strategies.

We have two sets of strategies. The first set adopted from (Papoudakis et al., 2021a) contains four heuristic strategies: pursuing the prey, following a randomly selected predator, approaching the nearest other agent, and moving toward the largest absolute relative-coordinate displacement among other agents. It also includes three pretrained IA2C (Papoudakis et al., 2021b) strategies, three pretrained MADDPG (Lowe et al., 2017), and observation-independent strategies (irrational strategies) that sample uniformly from the five available actions. Opponent tasks are formed by assigning a strategy to each of the three predator slots (Simulating the job of complete assignment 𝒳∈𝕏c\mathcal{X}\in\mathbb{X}_{c}).

Second, we construct a learned set of strategies with four training styles: direct, intercept, flank, and spread. Direct strategies use the environment reward without additional shaping. Intercept strategies are encouraged to approach the prey’s projected position using its current velocity, flank strategies are encouraged to approach from different directions, and spread strategies are encouraged to maintain greater separation between predators. These behaviors are encouraged through reward shaping with a coefficient of 0.05 rather than prescribed action rules. The set of strategies comprises IPPO training strategies with direct, intercept, and flank styles, plus held-out strategies covering new instances, the unseen spread style, and MAPPO (Yu et al., 2022) opponents. Check more details on the opponent strategy sets in Table 3.

E.2 Google Research Football (GRF)

Environment.

We use two scenarios in Google Research Football (Kurach et al., 2020): Academy Run to Score (R2S) with Keeper and a modified version of this scenario (R2S-DEF) and (R2S-4DEF). In both, the agent controls an attacker who starts near midfield with the ball and attempts to score against five defenders and a goalkeeper. In (R2S), all five defenders initially approach from behind the attacker. In (R2S-DEF), two defenders start between the attacker and the goal, while the remaining three approach from behind. and In (R2S-4DEF), four defenders start between the attacker and the goal, while the one remaining approach from behind. We cap episodes at 200 steps in both scenarios, with earlier termination following a goal, the ball leaving play, or a change in possession.

Both scenarios use 19 discrete actions, including movement, passing, shooting, sprinting, dribbling, and tackling. Observations use the 115-dimensional embedding, containing player positions and movement directions, ball information, possession, the active player, and the game mode. In the partially observed setting, opponent positions and movement directions are available within a Euclidean distance of 0.6 in normalized coordinates; otherwise, these values are replaced with -5.

Learning set of Strategies.

We construct separate strategy sets for the R2S, R2S-DEF, R2S-4DEF GRF scenarios by pretraining six-player teams against the built-in football AI. Each team contains five outfield players and a goalkeeper, with separate strategies for each player. Every strategy uses a feed-forward network with two 64-unit ReLU hidden layers, mapping a 115-dimensional observation to a categorical distribution over 19 actions. Teams train for one million environment steps with independent random seeds. IPPO uses a separate critic for each player, whereas MAPPO (Yu et al., 2022) uses a shared centralized critic during training.

All six players receive the same terminal reward: +1 for gaining possession, -1 for conceding a goal, and 0 for other episode endings. We add a small behavioral reward at each step, weighted by 0.001, to encourage different defensive styles. Low-block rewards favor positions near the penalty area and designated defensive locations. Medium-block rewards favor a defensive band farther from goal and discourage retreating into the penalty area. Pressing rewards encourage the three closest outfield players to approach the ball. Zonal rewards encourage players to follow assigned defensive regions that shift with the ball, together with a smaller incentive to apply pressure. For each scenario, the strategy set consists of IPPO teams exhibiting low-block, medium-block, and pressing tactics. Independently trained MAPPO teams (Yu et al., 2022), exhibiting low-block, medium-block, pressing, and zonal tactics, are reserved for evaluation. The exact opponent-strategy settings used in our experiments are shown in Table 4.

E.3 SMAC-HARD

Environment.

We use SMAC-HARD (Deng et al., 2024), an extension of the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) (Samvelyan et al., 2019). Whereas standard SMAC uses the built-in StarCraft II AI for the opposing team, SMAC-HARD provides multiplayer maps and an interface for externally controlled enemy strategies. It also introduces extensions for fog of war, unit abilities, terrain, and visibility. These features are inherited from SMAC-HARD. We extend SMAC-HARD by integrating PyMARL to train enemy-team strategies and deploy their frozen checkpoints as opponent populations. Our implementation supports learned, scripted, and built-in-AI opponents, with explicit task IDs defining controlled training and seen/unseen evaluation splits. We expose opponent action labels and physical features for auxiliary supervision while preserving the allied agents’ original observations. We synchronize all participating clients so that each environment transition advances exactly eight frames. Each episode starts with fresh, living teams, and simulation step and reset failures raise errors rather than being recorded as battle losses. Games are restarted between episodes when needed to avoid the simulation time limit, while preserving training progress. Evaluation preserves the training random-number states and performs no parameter updates. In our experiments, we use the 3s_vs_3z map, where the first team contains three Stalkers opposing three Zealots, the 3m map, where each team contains three Marines, and the 2s3z, where each team contains two Stalkers and three Zealots. Agents receive local SMAC observations and select available movement, stop, and targeted attack actions. The first-team agents are bound to existentially quantified variables, while the second-team agents are bound to universally quantified variables.

Learning set of Strategies.

We extend SMAC-HARD with an explicit opponent-task interface. Each task selects a complete enemy team at the beginning of an episode, and that team remains active throughout the battle. The interface supports scripted strategies, pretrained PyMARL (Samvelyan et al., 2019) teams, and native StarCraft II AI at different difficulty levels (i.e. 8, 9, 10). We additionally integrate PyMARL with the enemy side, enabling teams trained using VDN, QMIX, and QTRAN to be deployed as fixed opponents. The exact opponent-strategy settings used in our experiments are shown in Table 5.

Appendix F Additional Experimental Results

F.1 SLICR vs. LIAM

Fig. 7 compares SLICR and LIAM on PP using a new population of opponent strategies constructed with IPPO and MAPPO. In the Seen setting, SLICR (green line) performs similarly to LIAM (blue line) during most of the training process. However, during the final training steps, SLICR achieves up to ↑200{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt200} more single predator-prey collisions. In the Unseen setting, the advantage is more substantial, with SLICR (red line) achieving up to ↑500{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt500} more single predator-prey collisions than LIAM (orange line) during the final training steps.

We also report the number of eliminated agents bound to universally quantified variables in Fig. 8 and existentially quantified variables in Fig. 9. As shown in Fig. 8(c) in 3s_vs_3z map, SLICR (green line) eliminates all agents bound to universally quantified variables in the Seen setting. In the Unseen setting, SLICR (red line) eliminates nearly all such agents, whereas LIAM (orange line) eliminates only approximately half of them. Similarly, on the 3s_vs_3z map (see Fig. 9(c)), SLICR (green line) preserves two agents bound to existentially quantified variables in the Seen setting. In the Unseen setting, SLICR (red line) preserves approximately two agents, whereas LIAM (orange line) loses nearly all of them.

F.2 SLICR ∀∗∃∗\forall^{*}\exists^{*} vs. ∃∗∀∗\exists^{*}\forall^{*}

As shown in Table 1, on PP, GRF R2S, and GRF R2S-DEF, SLICR (∀∗∃∗\forall^{*}\exists^{*}) (blue line), (orange line) performs significantly better than SLICR (∃∗∀∗\exists^{*}\forall^{*}) (green line), (red line) in both the Seen and Unseen settings. Although Table 1 shows that SLICR (∀∗∃∗\forall^{*}\exists^{*}) and SLICR (∃∗∀∗\exists^{*}\forall^{*}) achieve similar overall performance on the SMAC-HARD scenarios, their learning curves reveal important differences. As shown in Figs. 10(d), 10(e) and 10(f), SLICR (∀∗∃∗\forall^{*}\exists^{*}) (blue line), (orange line) converges faster and achieves better results than SLICR (∃∗∀∗\exists^{*}\forall^{*}) (green line), (red line) on the 3m map in both the Seen and Unseen settings.

The results show that the shield improves the performance of SLICR across all considered proportions of irrational strategies. In particular, when 50%50\% of the strategies are irrational (blue line), the shield enables SLICR to achieve up to ↑250{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt250} more single-predator collisions, with an average gain of approximately ↑100{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt100}. When the strategy set contains 40%40\% (orange line) or 30%30\% (green line) irrational strategies, the performance gains are smaller but still reach up to ↑150{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt150} additional single-predator collisions. Finally, when 20%20\% of the strategies are irrational (red line), the shield continues to provide a positive average performance gain over SLICR without the shield.

F.4 Inner-LTL vs. Shaped Reward.

In addition to GRF R2S-DEF, where we investigate the effect of inner-LTL guidance. In Fig. 12, we conduct the same analysis on the GRF R2S scenario. In the Seen setting (blue line), inner-LTL of formula φR2S\varphi_{\text{R2S}} guidance achieves up to ↑10{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt10} more goals than the shaped reward. However, in the Unseen setting (orange line), the shaped reward performs better during most of training, with inner-LTL guidance outperforming it only between 2M and 2.5M training steps. We conduct similar experiments on the SMAC-HARD benchmarks. On the 3m map (see Fig. 13), inner-LTL guidance achieves up to a ↑18%{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt18\%} higher win rate early in training in the Seen setting (blue line). However, the gain becomes negligible once both SLICR and SLICR without inner-LTL guidance reach nearly 100%100\% win rates. Similarly, on the 2s3z map (see Fig. 14), inner-LTL guidance achieves gains of up to ↑25%{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt25\%} and ↑20%{\color[rgb]{0.0391,0.5352,0.2578}\uparrow\hskip-2.84526pt20\%} early in training in the Seen (blue line) and Unseen (orange line) settings, respectively. After approximately 200K training steps, both variants reach nearly 100%100\% win rates, and their performance becomes similar.

Appendix G Computational Resources

The experimental platform consisted of two AMD EPYC 7742 processors with 128 physical cores and 256 threads, approximately 1 TiB of RAM, and three NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q Workstation Edition GPUs with 96 GB of memory each.
